name: JFET Clean Boost
notes: One JFET in common source with a bypassed source resistor: up to about 20 dB of clean gain.

name: Single-Transistor Boost
notes: One silicon transistor in common emitter with a small emitter resistor: about 25 dB of gain, enough to push the next pedal or the amp into overdrive. The simplest pedal there is.

name: MOSFET Boost
notes: One small MOSFET in common source. Gain sets how much of the source resistor is bypassed, from about 4 dB to over 30 dB. The very high input impedance keeps the guitar's treble, and when pushed it clips softly and unevenly, a little like a tube.

name: Germanium Treble Booster
notes: One germanium PNP transistor with a tiny input capacitor, so it boosts treble far more than bass. Made to push a dark British valve amp into singing overdrive. Positive ground, −9 V supply.

name: Diode Overdrive
notes: Non-inverting op-amp stage with silicon diodes in the feedback loop (soft clipping), a treble-cut tone control and an output level.

name: Cascaded JFET Overdrive
notes: Three JFET gain stages in a row, laid out like the preamp of a valve amp. JFETs clip softly and unevenly much as triodes do, so this gives amp-like overdrive at 9 V.

name: Selectable-Clip Overdrive
notes: An op-amp overdrive with a three-way Clip selector in its feedback loop. A: two back-to-back MOSFETs, which clip late and softly (open, amp-like). B: two silicon diodes, which clip early (compressed, more driven). Centre: no clipping parts, a clean boost until the op-amp itself runs out of swing.

name: Hard-Clip Distortion
notes: An op-amp gain stage (up to about 200×) followed by two germanium diodes to ground, which chop the signal off at ±0.3 V: the bright, raw hard clipping of the first op-amp distortion pedals of the 1970s.

name: Slew-Limited Distortion
notes: A slow op-amp (0.3 V/µs) asked for up to 2000× gain: it can't keep up with the treble, which rounds the signal before two silicon diodes clip it. Filter turns the treble down as you turn it up. The sound of the late-1970s rodent-named distortion.

name: Two-Transistor Fuzz
notes: Two directly coupled transistors with feedback bias through R3. Fuzz sets how much emitter degeneration is bypassed.

name: Germanium Fuzz
notes: The 1960s round fuzz: two leaky germanium PNP transistors, directly coupled, on a −9 V supply (positive ground). It cleans up when you turn the guitar down, because its input impedance is low enough to load the pickups.

name: Four-Stage Sustain Fuzz
notes: The big, endless-sustain fuzz of the 1970s: a booster, then two stages that each clip with a pair of diodes in their feedback path, then a tone control that fades between a bass-only and a treble-only path (which scoops the middle), then a recovery stage.

name: Bass Blend Overdrive
notes: Made for bass. A buffer splits the signal in two: the drive path only adds gain above about 150 Hz, so the low notes stay solid while the mids and top break up, and Blend mixes it with the untouched clean signal. Fully clean at Blend 0, all drive at 10.

name: Four-Stage Phaser
notes: Four all-pass stages, each an op-amp with a capacitor and a JFET: the JFET, biased just above pinch-off, is a resistor whose value the LFO sweeps, so every stage's phase shift slides up and down the spectrum. Mixed half and half with the dry signal, the shifts cancel at two frequencies and the notches swoosh. The same plan as the classic one-knob orange phaser.

name: Opto Tremolo
notes: The LFO's triangle drives a transistor that lights the LED inside a vactrol. The light-dependent resistor sealed in with it shunts the guitar signal to ground, so the volume dips each time the LED brightens. The cell brightens quickly but darkens slowly, which gives the soft, lopsided throb of an amp's optical tremolo. Depth sets how much resistance stays in series with the cell.

name: Bucket-Brigade Chorus
notes: A 1024-stage bucket-brigade chip delays the guitar by about 7 ms; the LFO slides the chip's clock up and down, so the delay, and with it the pitch, wavers. Mixed half and half with the dry signal it doubles and shimmers. Op-amp low-pass filters either side of the chip keep its clock out of the audio, as in the real pedals, and the chip's own sampling and hiss are part of the model.

name: Bucket-Brigade Delay
notes: A 4096-stage bucket-brigade chip makes echoes from 20 ms to about 300 ms: Time sets its clock (slower clock, longer delay). The echo goes back through the inverting mixer at the front for the repeats, and every pass goes through the chip and its two low-pass filters, so each repeat comes back darker and grainier than the last, which is the sound of an analog delay. Turn Time while it plays for the pitch-bending warble of a real one.
